lesson.title: Count and Index: The Only Two Tuple Methods
lesson.summary: Tuples support just count() and index() because every method that would change a tuple in place, like append or sort, would violate the immutability that defines them.
lesson.body:
Lists come with a long list of methods: append, remove, sort, insert, extend, and more. Tuples come with exactly two: count() and index(). This is not an oversight; it follows directly from Tuple Immutability. Every one of those list methods either adds, removes, or reorders elements in place, and a tuple, by definition, cannot be changed in place at all. There is simply nothing for an append() or a sort() to do on a tuple that would not break the promise that makes a tuple a tuple.

What is left are the two operations that only read a tuple without ever trying to modify it: counting how many times a value appears, and finding the position of a value's first occurrence.

grades = (85, 90, 85, 78, 85, 92)
print(grades.count(85))
print(grades.index(90))

This prints 3, because 85 appears three times in grades, and then 1, because the first 90 sits at index 1 (grades[0] is 85, grades[1] is 90). Like a list's index() method, tuple.index() raises an error rather than returning some placeholder value if the item is not present at all.

try:
    grades.index(100)
except ValueError as e:
    print("Error:", e)

This prints Error: tuple.index(x): x not in tuple, since 100 never appears in grades.

If you do need a sorted or rearranged version of a tuple's contents, you reach for a built-in function instead of a method, since the function can build and return a brand new object rather than modifying the tuple: sorted(grades) returns the list [78, 85, 85, 85, 90, 92], leaving the original tuple grades completely untouched.
